Incorporating SLOOS alongside the FOMC’s March 15, 2020 actions and the Financial Stability Report points to a deeper near-term drag via the bank credit channel. Banks reported tightening across key categories—C&I loans (including tighter other terms across firm sizes), construction and land development, and elements of consumer credit (higher credit score thresholds, tighter credit limits, reduced loan granting). Demand weakened notably for construction and some consumer loans, and banks signaled reduced risk tolerance and expectations of deterioration in loan performance, collateral values, HELOCs, and small-firm/syndicated loan performance. Many banks also expected tighter standards to persist through 2020.

These SLOOS findings reinforce downside risks to activity and credit supply beyond the COVID shock itself, compounding the financial fragilities highlighted in the FSR. While strong bank capital/liquidity and the Fed’s swift move to the ELB, large-scale Treasury/agency MBS purchases, expanded repos, and dollar swap lines help stabilize markets and ease funding strains, the prospective tightening in lending standards suggests a more pronounced and persistent headwind to credit availability.

Net: outlook tilts more negative than the initial read; policy support mitigates tail risks, but SLOOS-implied credit tightening warrants a lower sentiment reading.
